mode: sentence-initial character name (Sally, Lila, Lily) starting a new sentence after dialogue or narration
sentence-initial 'The' starting a sentence right after a happy or proud scene
sentence-initial 'Her' before mom, dad, mum or uncle in family scenes
period ending a sentence that names a feeling: 'brighter.', 'put it on.', 'was sad.'
noun ending a descriptive phrase: 'eyes', 'containers', 'views', 'success', 'summer'
'They' or 'sisters' starting a sentence after a group fun or outing scene
'to' or 'told' after speech verbs: 'said to', 'says to', 'told the other animals'
clause-starting 'whose', 'says', or 'It' in mixed narration, code, and dialogue text

summary: Fires on sentence-level function tokens in children's stories (character names, pronouns, 'to' after speech verbs, sentence-end periods) rather than on feeling words; mostly not emotion-related, though two modes sit in happy or feeling-laden scenes.

mode: 'the' after 'of' or 'for' in dark, tense story text: 'weight of the', 'empathy for the'
'He', 'She', 'plane' starting a story's main clause after 'Once upon a time, there was'
'and', 'would', 'escape', 'boy', ',' ending a triumphant or hopeful clause: 'a hero and', 'they would always'
copula 'was', 'is', 'were', 'so' right before 'happy' or 'glad' describing the character
'!', '.', or quote mark closing a gratitude or happy line: 'happy to help!', 'nurse.'
'What' opening a screenplay question line; 'Fre' mid-name in plain narration

summary: Fires on function words and punctuation in story text, most strongly just before or after happy or grateful phrasing (copula before 'happy', punctuation after 'I'm glad I could help'); partly emotion-related, mostly happy and gratitude.

mode: period or 'excited'/'happy' after a joyful reaction: 'started to laugh.', 'overjoyed.', 'was so happy'
DUPLICATE: 'am', 'I', 'not' in Socrates' gadfly speech: 'I am the gadfly', 'I am not going'
'such' and 'Law' in legal or religious text; 'fast' in Socrates' gadfly speech

summary: Fires on sentence endings and feeling adjectives after joyful reactions in short stories, and on 'I am' self-description in one Socrates passage; only the happy-reaction mode is emotion-related.

mode: last word of a positive phrase: 'smiled with pride', 'softly and kindly', 'explore this magical place'
hyphen inside ISBN numbers, e.g. '0-231-10936-9' in book citations
digit '6' in IP address 220.127.116.11 and 'uta' in forum-post text

summary: Fires on hyphens in ISBN numbers, digits in IP addresses, and the final word of some positive story phrases such as 'smiled with pride'; not emotion-specific.

mode: 'He', 'he', 'She', 'They' starting a clause after a character is busy, tired, or sad
'want' in 'I want to play', 'I want to touch' when a child sees something fun
'not' in 'I do not have', 'to' in 'easy to memorize', 'there' in 'if there are'

summary: Fires on 'I want' desire statements and narrative subject pronouns in children's stories; desire is not one of the listed emotions, so not emotion-related.

mode: 'was', 'Ben', 'Lily', 'and', 'Jack' starting clauses in playground or animal scenes
'i', ')', '.' inside Poe-style love-poem lines: 'I love thee', 'my darling'
'€' mojibake after a cloudy-sky line; 'into' in Bible text; 's' in 'mom's makeup'

summary: Fires on clause-level tokens in children's stories and, most strongly, inside love-poem lines ('I love thee', 'my darling'); only the love-poem mode is emotion-related.

mode: comma after the story opener 'Once upon a time' before 'there was a girl named'
'They', 'they', 'Lily', or comma starting a sentence after a friendship or reunion
'was' in story openers 'Once upon a time, there was a little girl named'
'assistant' tag right after a user turn in chat transcripts

summary: Fires on story-opening 'Once upon a time, there was' tokens and on the subject after a friendship or reunion; a narrative-structure neuron, not emotion-related.

mode: 'noticed' or 'saw' after a character looks around or opens something: 'he noticed', 'she saw'
period ending a sentence about a scare or a joy: 'looked terrible.', 'laughed.', 'was locked.'
'mashed', 'cream', 'noise', 'and', 'size' in recipe sentences or story lines
'was' after 'It' describing an object: 'It was heading', 'It was dull green'
'she' or 'that' after yoga-benefit sentences: 'she naturally started', 'that her anxiety'
'separate', 'or', 'ular', 'B' in medical or animal-husbandry reference text
'very' before an adjective describing an object: 'very special', 'very high', 'very bright'
'She', 'He', 'It' starting a clause after a plot beat in a story, e.g. 'She quickly became worried'
'Suddenly', 'Then', or comma starting a plot-twist sentence in a children's story
''s', '9', 'Pest' in mixed how-to, dialogue, and reference text

summary: Fires on narrative transition and subject tokens in children's stories, plus 'very' before adjectives and some medical or recipe text; only the scare-or-joy sentence-end mode is loosely emotion-related.
